description: We are Team from Cali, Colombia: a small, multidisciplinary team led by Juan Jose Ruiz, a biomedical engineer with hands-on experience in clinical software development, biomedical infrastructure monitoring and digital architecture. We like building practical tools where health, data and technology meet.
summary: NAHI (Networked Astronaut Health Intelligence) is an offline-first crew health copilot for long-duration missions. On the way to Mars, a message to Earth can take 22 minutes one way, so astronauts must catch and act on health changes themselves. NAHI gathers data from wearables, cabin sensors, radiation references, exams and daily check-ins; compares each astronaut with their own preflight baseline and NASA standards; and turns every change into a proportional, explained action, from "repeat the measurement" to an authorized checklist. A deterministic six-step engine (quality gate, context, robust personal baseline, CUSUM persistence, multi-system corroboration and evidence-tiered rules) keeps false alarms low and makes every alert traceable; no AI model makes decisions. If a crew member stops responding to a watch check-in, the nearest crewmate's watch receives a step-by-step protocol while a compact case is queued for Earth. The prototype runs in the browser with desktop, compact and smartwatch views, role-based privacy, an on-device evidence library and a validation suite (8 of 8 scenarios detected). NAHI matters because autonomy, not more alarms, keeps crews safe when Earth can't answer in time.
details:
WHAT NAHI DOES

NAHI (Networked Astronaut Health Intelligence) is an offline-first crew health copilot for long-duration missions. It gathers health indicators, evaluates them against each astronaut's own baseline and NASA standards, and helps the crew act, even when the link to Earth is delayed by up to 22 minutes or completely down. NAHI does not diagnose: it detects change, explains it, states how certain it is, and proposes a proportional action.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Gather: every measurement (wearable vitals, cabin CO2, temperature and humidity, radiation dose, periodic exams, PVT-B reaction tests and daily check-ins) is stored as a FHIR-inspired observation with unit, time, device, context, signal quality and provenance (synthetic, NASA standard, reference data or user import).

2. Evaluate with a deterministic six-step engine:

- Quality gate: low-quality or implausible samples are dropped; under 70% coverage in the last 7 days is labeled "insufficient data", never "normal".

- Context: sleep is compared with sleep and rest with rest; exercise never triggers rest alerts.

- Personal baseline: 28 preflight days per metric, median and MAD, modified z-score (|Mz| >= 3.5 = transient change).

- Persistence: two-sided CUSUM (k = 0.5, h = 5; about one false signal per 465 days per metric) plus EWMA drift from the preflight baseline.

- Corroboration: clinical escalation only when two or more body systems change together, or when a NASA standard limit is reached.

- Evidence tiers: every rule is labeled NASA STANDARD (e.g., the 600 mSv career dose limit), ASSOCIATION (e.g., sleep under 6 h and slower PVT-B; cabin CO2 and headaches) or PROTOTYPE HEURISTIC.

3. Act: each alert shows the observation, explanation, evidence, allowed action and escalation level. Actions climb a ladder: 0 continue, 1 repeat measurement, 2 self-care, 3 consult the crew medical officer, 4 prioritize the flight surgeon, 5 run an authorized checklist. Levels 0-2 run automatically; levels 3-5 are auto-initiated but a human confirms each critical step; medication, invasive procedures and mission decisions always stay with humans.

Communication modes (connected, delayed 0-22 min, blackout) change what NAHI does with the flight surgeon's compact case package: send it, queue it or hold it. Autonomy can run in shadow, assisted or automatic mode. If an astronaut misses a watch check-in while their heart rate leaves their personal range or they stop moving, the watch raises an alarm and then sends a step-by-step protocol to the nearest crewmate's watch and notifies the medical officer.

WHAT THE PROTOTYPE INCLUDES

- LIVE view: real-time (simulated) vitals, cabin and radiation data, readiness for EVA (spacewalk), high-load exercise and critical operations, the priority alert, daily wellness tips and upcoming checks.

- One arrow opens the menu: Crew (commander view, readiness only, no clinical values), Clinical (detailed trends for the medical officer), History (traceable decisions), Functions (check-in, PVT-B test, guided breathing, routines and checklists), Knowledge · RAG (17 NASA and peer-reviewed sources, on-device retrieval only, no text generation), Scenarios, Validation, Settings and About.

- Desktop, compact and smartwatch views, plus a 30-second story mode.

BENEFITS

- Fewer false alarms: personal baselines, persistence and corroboration instead of fixed Earth thresholds.

- Trust: every alert is explainable and cites its evidence; missing data is never shown as normal.

- Autonomy: useful decisions without waiting for Earth.

- Privacy: role-based views (the commander sees readiness, not clinical numbers), which helps reduce under-reporting of symptoms.

INTENDED IMPACT

In space, NAHI supports the shift toward Earth-independent medical operations for lunar and Mars crews. On Earth, the same offline-first design can serve remote clinics with delayed access to specialists, such as rural communities in Colombia, and other isolated settings.

HOW WE VALIDATED IT

8 synthetic scenarios with known expected outcomes (8/8 detected), a 365-day in-control run (0.42 false signals per astronaut-month vs 0.33 predicted by theory) and a determinism check (same input, same output, same FNV-1a hash). This validates software coherence and traceability, not clinical efficacy.

TOOLS

React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui, with IBM Plex fonts. The app runs client-side in the browser and is hosted at nahi-space-app.com. It was built with Lovable from our written specifications; research and writing were supported by AI assistants (see Use of AI).

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- The buddy protocol: when someone stops responding, help comes from the nearest crewmate's watch, not from Earth.

- Uncertainty is a feature: evidence tiers and explicit "insufficient data" states instead of false confidence.

- Health is separated from mission readiness, so crews get useful guidance without diagnoses or exposing private data.

- A monochrome design where status is shown with patterns instead of colors, for readability and future low-power displays.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Communication delays and blackouts; alarm fatigue (72-99% of hospital clinical alarms are false); scientific honesty (ISS evidence is not Mars evidence, synthetic data is always labeled, and thresholds are prototype heuristics until validated); human-in-the-loop safety with overrides and traceability; crew privacy; interoperability (FHIR-inspired data model, HL7/FHIR planned); accessibility; and NASA branding rules (no NASA logos or insignia).

LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

NAHI is a prototype, not a medical device, and runs on synthetic data. Next: calibrate thresholds with analog-mission and bed-rest data, run in shadow mode next to flight surgeons, and connect real sensors (Bio-Monitor-class garments, dosimeters) through HL7/FHIR.
